name: ML Privacy & Model Security
description: Privacy attacks against ML (membership inference, model/data extraction, inversion) and federated-learning security.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, all from USENIX Security 2018, mark the moment when ML privacy and model security crystallized into a distinct research agenda. The work split along two lines that still organize the field. One line was defensive and protective: "AttriGuard: A Practical Defense Against Attribute Inference Attacks via Adversarial Machine Learning" (USENIX 2018) used adversarial perturbations to stop attackers from inferring users' hidden attributes, while "Turning Your Weakness Into a Strength: Watermarking Deep Neural Networks by Backdooring" (USENIX 2018) repurposed backdoors as a tool for claiming model ownership. The other line was offensive, exposing how much models leak: "With Great Training Comes Great Vulnerability: Practical Attacks against Transfer Learning" (USENIX 2018) showed that the now-common practice of fine-tuning shared backbones opens a clear attack surface, and "GAZELLE: A Low Latency Framework for Secure Neural Network Inference" (USENIX 2018) began the parallel effort to run inference without exposing data at all.

Around 2019-2020 the field grew more rigorous and more physical. "Evaluating Differentially Private Machine Learning in Practice" (USENIX 2019) pushed past theory to ask what a privacy budget really buys, becoming a reference point for honest accounting of DP defenses. At the same time, attackers moved off the math and onto the hardware: "CSI NN: Reverse Engineering of Neural Network Architectures Through Electromagnetic Side Channel" (USENIX 2019) and "Stealthy Tracking of Autonomous Vehicles with Cache Side Channels" (USENIX 2020) showed that side channels can steal architectures and track real systems. "Fawkes: Protecting Privacy against Unauthorized Deep Learning Models" (USENIX 2020) turned the protective instinct toward ordinary users, cloaking photos against facial recognition scrapers like Clearview.ai.

By 2022-2023 attention shifted decisively toward distributed training and generative models, and the volume of work exploded. Federated and split learning became a battleground: "FLAME: Taming Backdoors in Federated Learning" (USENIX 2022) defended the global model, while attacks like "VILLAIN: Backdoor Attacks Against Vertical Split Learning" (USENIX 2023) and "PCAT: Functionality and Data Stealing from Split Learning by Pseudo-Client Attack" (USENIX 2023) showed that splitting a model does not by itself protect the data inside it. Generative models brought their own crisis of memorization: "Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models" (USENIX 2023), one of the most-cited papers here, demonstrated that image generators regurgitate their training data verbatim, and "CodexLeaks: Privacy Leaks from Code Generation Language Models in GitHub Copilot" (USENIX 2023) showed the same problem for code models in production.

Most recently the field has been responding to the dominance of large generative and foundation models on both the attack and defense sides. Defenses now aim to make generation itself private, as in "dp-promise: Differentially Private Diffusion Probabilistic Models for Image Synthesis" (USENIX 2024), and to harden deployed APIs against theft, as in "ModelGuard: Information-Theoretic Defense Against Model Extraction Attacks" (USENIX 2024). Cryptographic verifiability has matured from the inference frameworks of GAZELLE into scalable proofs, with "Scalable Zero-knowledge Proofs for Non-linear Functions in Machine Learning" (USENIX 2024). And the classic membership-inference question that animated the early work has been carried into the LLM era by "Towards Label-Only Membership Inference Attack against Pre-trained Large Language Models" (USENIX 2025), showing that even with only label access, one can probe what a large model has seen. The throughline across all these venues is a steady escalation: each new training paradigm and model class reopens the same privacy questions on harder terrain.

milestones.note: founding work that repurposed backdoors as a model-ownership watermark, seeding a long line of model-protection research

milestones.note: brought rigorous, practical accounting to what differential privacy actually buys, becoming a reference point for honest DP evaluation

milestones.note: shifted privacy protection to ordinary users by cloaking photos against unauthorized facial-recognition scrapers

milestones.note: anchored the federated-learning security agenda with a practical defense against backdoor poisoning of the global model

milestones.note: most-cited entry here; proved generative diffusion models memorize and regurgitate training images verbatim, defining the generative-memorization threat

milestones.note: showed that split learning does not inherently protect client data, exposing a core weakness in distributed-training privacy

milestones.note: matured deployed-API defense with an information-theoretic guard against model extraction from MLaaS query interfaces

milestones.note: carried the classic membership-inference question into the LLM era under the restrictive label-only access setting

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list splits along two lines that would define the field. On the attack side, "Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks" (NDSS 2018) showed that shared, publicly distributed models could be quietly subverted, while a cluster of 2018 papers turned the lens on what models leak: "Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks" (CCS 2018) and "Stealing Hyperparameters in Machine Learning" (S&P 2018) demonstrated that even abstract properties and training settings could be recovered from a model. In parallel, defenders began responding both with empirical patches like "Machine Learning with Membership Privacy using Adversarial Regularization" (CCS 2018) and "AttriGuard" (USENIX 2018), and with cryptographic privacy via secure inference systems such as "GAZELLE" (USENIX 2018) and "Secure Outsourced Matrix Computation" (CCS 2018).

The 2019 wave sharpened membership and inference attacks into a science and pushed them into the collaborative setting. "Comprehensive Privacy Analysis of Deep Learning" (S&P 2019) and "Exploiting Unintended Feature Leakage in Collaborative Learning" (S&P 2019) showed that federated and centralized training both leak, including through white-box and active adversaries — connecting privacy leakage directly to the distributed-training agenda that would later dominate. This period also matured the defense toolkit: differential privacy moved from theory to scrutiny with "Evaluating Differentially Private Machine Learning in Practice" (USENIX 2019) and "Differentially Private Model Publishing for Deep Learning" (S&P 2019), trojan detection emerged with "ABS" (CCS 2019), and "Neural Network Inversion in Adversarial Setting" (CCS 2019) extended leakage to reconstructing inputs. A recurring theme — that defenses can backfire — appeared in "Privacy Risks of Securing Machine Learning Models against Adversarial Examples" (CCS 2019).

By 2020-2021 the targets broadened from classifiers to generative and language models, and the field grew more self-critical. "GAN-Leaks" (CCS 2020), "Information Leakage in Embedding Models" (CCS 2020), and "Privacy Risks of General-Purpose Language Models" (S&P 2020) extended membership and reconstruction attacks to GANs, embeddings, and large LMs, while "Fawkes" (USENIX 2020) turned privacy attacks into a user-facing protection against facial recognition. "Machine Unlearning" (S&P 2021) opened the right-to-be-forgotten subfield, immediately complicated by "When Machine Unlearning Jeopardizes Privacy" (CCS 2021). Federated learning security crystallized around poisoning attacks and defenses with "Manipulating the Byzantine" (NDSS 2021), and "Adversary Instantiation" (S&P 2021) reframed DP guarantees as concrete lower bounds.

The current frontier, reflected in 2022-2023, is rigor and scale. "Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles" (S&P 2022) and "Enhanced Membership Inference Attacks" (CCS 2022) re-grounded the canonical attack in proper statistical evaluation, while federated defenses were stress-tested by "Back to the Drawing Board" (S&P 2022) against the more practical mitigations "FLAME" (USENIX 2022) and "DeepSight" (NDSS 2022). Most strikingly, "Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models" (USENIX 2023) and "Analyzing Leakage of Personally Identifiable Information in Language Models" (S&P 2023) showed that today's largest generative models memorize and regurgitate verbatim training data — moving the field from "can we infer membership?" to "we can extract the data itself," now the dominant concern for foundation models.

milestones.title: Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks
milestones.note: established the threat that shared, public neural-network models can be covertly backdoored, seeding the trojan/backdoor research line

milestones.title: Stealing Hyperparameters in Machine Learning
milestones.note: showed that even abstract training details could be extracted from a deployed model, broadening the model-extraction threat model

milestones.title: Comprehensive Privacy Analysis of Deep Learning: Passive and Active White-box Inference Attacks against Centralized and Federated Learning
milestones.note: systematized white-box and active membership inference across both centralized and federated training, linking leakage to collaborative learning

milestones.title: Privacy Risks of General-Purpose Language Models
milestones.note: extended privacy leakage from classifiers to large general-purpose language models, presaging the LLM-memorization concerns that dominate today

milestones.title: Machine Unlearning
milestones.note: launched the machine-unlearning subfield by formalizing efficient data deletion from trained models

milestones.title: Manipulating the Byzantine: Optimizing Model Poisoning Attacks and Defenses for Federated Learning
milestones.note: crystallized the federated-learning poisoning attack-and-defense arms race with optimized, principled attacks

milestones.title: Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles
milestones.note: re-grounded membership inference in rigorous low-false-positive statistical evaluation, setting the modern benchmark standard

milestones.title: Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models
milestones.note: proved that state-of-the-art generative models verbatim-memorize and regurgitate training images, shifting the field from inference to direct data extraction
